# ANS - Lexer & Parser (D2, Part 1)

A hand-written C lexer and recursive-descent parser for the ANS (Alchemist's Notation Script) domain-specific language.

---

## Build

```
make          # optimised build
make debug    # add -g -DDEBUG
```

Requires a C11 compiler (`cc`).  No external dependencies.

---

## Run

```
./ans <file.ans>                  # parse; exit 0 on success, 1 on error
./ans --dump-ast <file.ans>       # parse and print the AST
```

---

## Test

```
make test
```

Runs all programs in `tests/valid/` (each must exit 0) and all programs in `tests/invalid/` (each must exit 1).

---

## Error format

```
<file>:<line>:<col>: error: <message>
```

Example:

```
tests/invalid/missing_semicolon.ans:8:1: error: expected ';' but got let
```

The parser uses panic-mode recovery (skips to the next `;`, `}`, or EOF) so multiple errors can be reported in a single run.

---

## AST dump example

```
$ ./ans --dump-ast tests/valid/elements.ans
Program
├── ElementDecl [H]
│   ├── ElementField [atomic_mass]
│   │   └── Number [1.008]
│   ├── ElementField [valence]
│   │   └── Number [1]
│   └── ElementField [symbol]
│       └── String ["H"]
...
```

---

## Project layout

```
D2/
├── Makefile
├── README.md
├── include/
│   ├── lexer.h     token types, Token struct, Lexer API
│   ├── parser.h    Parser struct, parse_program
│   ├── ast.h       NodeKind enum, AstNode, ast_* API
│   └── error.h     error_at / fatal_at
├── src/
│   ├── main.c      CLI entry point
│   ├── lexer.c     maximal-munch scanner
│   ├── parser.c    recursive-descent parser (one function per EBNF rule)
│   ├── ast.c       node constructors + tree pretty-printer
│   └── error.c     error formatting
└── tests/
    ├── valid/      8 programs — must all be accepted
    └── invalid/    4 programs — must all be rejected
```

---

## Authors

Yusuf Hamza Çelebi · Enes Özkan  
CSE 341 — Programming Languages, Gebze Technical University, Spring 2026

10	
11	User-defined names for variables, functions, compounds, and reactions.
12

15	```
16

18

22

28	```

32	```

34	```
35	Examples: `"Hydrogen"`, `"Water"`, `"Carbon dioxide"`
36	
37	#### Character literal
38	```
39	'(?:[^'\\\r\n]|\\['\\nrt])'
40	```
41	Examples: `'H'`, `'\n'`
42	
43	#### Formula literal
44	```
45	(?:[A-Z][a-z]?(?:[1-9][0-9]*)?)+
46	```
47	Examples: `H`, `O`, `H2O`, `CH4`, `CO2`, `O2`
48	
49	> **Note — subscript 1:** The pattern accepts a subscript of 1, so `H1` is a lexically valid formula literal. A token sequence like `H1O` is lexed as two consecutive formula literals (`H1` and `O`), which the semantic phase rejects as a malformed compound formula.
50	
51	#### Unit literal (compound forms only)
52	```
53	kg/mol | g/mol | kJ/mol
54	```
55	Examples: `g/mol`, `kg/mol`, `kJ/mol`

57	These three tokens contain `/` and therefore can never be valid identifiers. The lexer recognises them by simple pattern priority over the `/` operator — a straightforward longest-match rule, with no lookahead or lexer statefulness required.
58

60

63	<unit>                       → UNIT_LITERAL | "mol" | "g" | "kg" | "kJ"
64	```
65	
66	handles the pairing entirely at the parser level.
67

85	|---|---|

106

111	```
112	
113	Pattern: `[{}()\[\],;.]`
114

116

120	|---|---|---|

122	| Whitespace | `[ \t\f\r\n]+` | Token separator only; not a token |

---

## Token Categories

### 1. Identifiers

User-defined names for variables, functions, compounds, and reactions.

```
[a-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*
```

Examples: `water`, `mass`, `compute_yield`, `reactant_mol`

---

#### Number literal
```
(?:0|[1-9][0-9]*)(?:\.[0-9]+)?(?:[eE][+-]?[0-9]+)?
```
Examples: `20`, `1.008`, `21.2`, `890.3`, `6.02e23`

#### String literal
```
"(?:[^"\\\r\n]|\\["\\nrt])*"
```
Examples: `"Hydrogen"`, `"Water"`, `"Carbon dioxide"`

#### Character literal
```
'(?:[^'\\\r\n]|\\['\\nrt])'
```
Examples: `'H'`, `'\n'`

#### Formula literal
```
(?:[A-Z][a-z]?(?:[1-9][0-9]*)?)+
```
Examples: `H`, `O`, `H2O`, `CH4`, `CO2`, `O2`

> **Note — subscript 1:** The pattern accepts a subscript of 1, so `H1` is a lexically valid formula literal. In standard chemistry `H` and `H1` denote the same species; the semantic checker normalises `H1` to `H`. A token sequence like `H1O` is lexed as two consecutive formula literals (`H1` and `O`), which the semantic phase rejects as a malformed compound formula.

#### Unit literal (compound forms only)
```
kg/mol | g/mol | kJ/mol
```
Examples: `g/mol`, `kg/mol`, `kJ/mol`

These three tokens contain `/` and therefore can never be valid identifiers. The lexer recognises them by simple pattern priority over the `/` operator — a straightforward longest-match rule, with no lookahead or lexer statefulness required.

The parser promotes them to a `<unit>` role only when they directly follow a number literal inside a `<number_or_quantity_literal>` or `<quantity_literal>` rule. Everywhere else (function parameters, property names, arithmetic expressions) they remain plain identifiers. This removes any need for a stateful or context-sensitive lexer: the `5.0 mol` sequence is tokenised as `NUMBER_LITERAL IDENTIFIER`, and the grammar rule

```
<number_or_quantity_literal> → <number_literal> [ <unit> ]
<unit>                       → UNIT_LITERAL | "mol" | "g" | "kg" | "kJ"
```

handles the pairing entirely at the parser level.

> **Notation note:** the quoted alternatives `"mol"`, `"g"`, `"kg"`, `"kJ"` in the `<unit>` rule match an `IDENTIFIER` token whose lexeme equals that string — they are not a separate token class. The lexer emits `IDENTIFIER` in all four cases; the parser accepts the token by lexeme value, exactly as it does for other contextual keywords such as `"balanced"` and `"exothermic"`.

---

### 3. Keywords

The scanner always produces an `IDENTIFIER` token for every word-shaped lexeme. A **reserved-word filter** (outside the FA proper) then promotes tokens to `KEYWORD` if their lexeme is in the hard reserved-word table — the standard technique described by Sebesta (§5.1). Contextual keywords are promoted further by the **parser** based on grammar position.

#### Hard reserved words — may never be used as identifiers

```
let  function  return  for  in  if  elif  else  print
```

#### Contextual keywords — promoted by the parser, not the lexer

| Grammar position | Words |
|---|---|
| Declaration head | `element`  `compound`  `reaction` |
| Declaration field names | `atomic_mass`  `valence`  `symbol`  `formula`  `name`  `reactants`  `products`  `check`  `energy` |
| Reaction field values | `balanced`  `exothermic`  `endothermic` |
| Parameter type annotations | `element`  `compound`  `reaction` |

Because promotion is done by the parser, the parser resolves which role applies from surrounding grammar context: immediately following `function … (` and preceding a bare identifier → type annotation; at the start of a top-level statement → declaration keyword. The scanner emits the same `IDENTIFIER` token in both cases.

---

### 4. Operators

```

```

---

```

```

---

| Category | Pattern | Notes |
|---|---|---|

1	(*
2	ANS Complete EBNF Grammar
3	Sebesta-style notation for the implemented C-like ANS subset.
4	
5	Conventions:
6	  <nonterminal> → production
7	  terminal      means exact source text (shown in lowercase or quoted)
8	  { X }         means zero or more repetitions of X
9	  [ X ]         means optional X
10	  ( X | Y )     means one of the alternatives X or Y
11	  |             separates top-level alternatives in a rule
12	  EOF           means end of file
13	
14	Important lexer convention:
15	  ANS uses contextual chemistry words. Lowercase words are first tokenized
16	  as IDENTIFIER-like words. The parser interprets words such as element,
17	  compound, reaction, formula, reactants, products, balanced, exothermic,
18	  and endothermic as special words only in grammar positions where they
19	  have special meaning. This allows typed parameters such as:
20	
21	      function compute_yield(reaction r, compound c) { ... };
22	      function molar_mass(compound c) { ... };
23	*)
24	
25	(* ============================================================
26	   1. Program Structure
27	   ============================================================ *)
28	
29	<program> → { <top_level_statement> } EOF
30	
31	<top_level_statement> → <element_declaration> ";"
32	                      | <compound_declaration> ";"
33	                      | <reaction_declaration> ";"
34	                      | <function_declaration> ";"
35	                      | <variable_declaration> ";"
36	                      | <assignment_statement> ";"
37	                      | <augmented_assignment_statement> ";"
38	                      | <print_statement> ";"
39	                      | <expression_statement> ";"
40	                      | <if_statement>
41	
42	(* ============================================================
43	   2. General Statements and Blocks
44	   ============================================================ *)
45	
46	<block> → "{" { <statement> } "}"
47	
48	<statement> → <variable_declaration> ";"
49	            | <assignment_statement> ";"
50	            | <augmented_assignment_statement> ";"
51	            | <return_statement> ";"
52	            | <print_statement> ";"
53	            | <expression_statement> ";"
54	            | <for_statement>
55	            | <if_statement>
56	
57	<variable_declaration> → "let" <identifier> "=" <expression>
58	
59	<assignment_statement> → <assignable> "=" <expression>
60	
61	<augmented_assignment_statement> → <assignable> <augmented_assignment_operator> <expression>
62	
63	<augmented_assignment_operator> → "+=" | "-=" | "*=" | "/="
64	
65	<return_statement> → "return" [ <expression> ]
66	
67	<print_statement> → "print" <expression>
68	
69	<expression_statement> → <expression>
70	
71	(* ============================================================
72	   3. Function Declarations
73	   ============================================================ *)
74	
75	<function_declaration> → "function" <identifier> "(" [ <parameter_list> ] ")" <block>
76	
77	<parameter_list> → <parameter> { "," <parameter> }
78	
79	<parameter> → [ <type_name> ] <identifier>
80	
81	<type_name> → "element" | "compound" | "reaction"
82	
83	(* Typed parameters allow the type-checker to verify that the correct kind of
84	   value is passed at call sites. The type annotation is optional; untyped
85	   parameters accept any value. Examples:
86	       reaction r    compound c    element e    mol (untyped)
87	
88	   Ambiguity resolution:
89	   element, compound, and reaction are parsed as <type_name> only when they
90	   immediately precede an <identifier> inside a <parameter_list>. Elsewhere
91	   these words may still appear as identifiers. *)
92	
93	(* ============================================================
94	   4. For Loops
95	   ============================================================ *)
96	
97	<for_statement> → "for" "(" "let" <identifier> "in" <expression> ")" <block>
98	
99	(* Example:
100	   for (let element in formula) {
101	       mass += element.atomic_mass * formula[element];
102	   }
103	*)
104	
105	(* ============================================================
106	   5. If / Elif / Else Statements
107	   ============================================================ *)
108	
109	<if_statement> → "if" "(" <expression> ")" <block>
110	                 { <elif_clause> } [ <else_clause> ]
111	
112	<elif_clause> → "elif" "(" <expression> ")" <block>
113	
114	<else_clause> → "else" <block>
115	
116	(* Conditions are always wrapped in parentheses, matching the for-loop style.
117	
118	   Dangling-else resolution:
119	   Every branch body is a braced <block>, so the classic unbraced ambiguity
120	       if a if b s else t
121	   cannot arise. The optional <else_clause> belongs to the nearest preceding
122	   <if_statement>. *)
123	
124	(* ============================================================
125	   6. Element Declarations
126	   ============================================================ *)
127	
128	<element_declaration> → "element" <element_symbol> "{" <element_field_list> "}"
129	
130	<element_symbol> → <formula_literal>
131	
132	<element_field_list> → <element_field> { "," <element_field> } [ "," ]
133	
134	<element_field> → "atomic_mass" "=" <number_literal>
135	                | "valence"     "=" <number_literal>
136	                | "symbol"      "=" <string_literal>
137	
138	(* Semantic requirements:
139	   - <element_symbol> must be a single valid periodic-table symbol (e.g., H).
140	   - The element body must contain atomic_mass, valence, and symbol exactly once.
141	   - Duplicate or missing fields are semantic errors, not syntax errors.
142	   H is lexically a <formula_literal>; after "element" it is an element symbol. *)
143	
144	(* ============================================================
145	   7. Compound Declarations
146	   ============================================================ *)
147	
148	<compound_declaration> → "compound" <identifier> "{" <compound_field_list> "}"
149	
150	<compound_field_list> → <compound_field> { "," <compound_field> } [ "," ]
151	
152	<compound_field> → "formula" "=" <formula_literal>
153	                 | "name"    "=" <string_literal>
154	
155	(* Semantic requirements:
156	   - The compound body must contain formula and name exactly once.
157	   - Every element symbol inside <formula_literal> must refer to a declared
158	     or built-in element. *)
159	
160	(* ============================================================
161	   8. Reaction Declarations
162	   ============================================================ *)
163	
164	<reaction_declaration> → "reaction" <identifier> "{" <reaction_field_list> "}"
165	
166	<reaction_field_list> → <reaction_field> { "," <reaction_field> } [ "," ]
167	
168	<reaction_field> → "reactants" "=" <reaction_expression>
169	                 | "products"  "=" <reaction_expression>
170	                 | "check"     "=" <balance_check>
171	                 | "energy"    "=" <energy_expression>
172	
173	<balance_check> → "balanced"
174	
175	<energy_expression> → <energy_kind> <quantity_literal>
176	
177	<energy_kind> → "exothermic" | "endothermic"
178	
179	(* Semantic requirements:
180	   - The reaction body must contain reactants, products, check, and energy
181	     exactly once.
182	   - If check = balanced appears, the semantic checker verifies equal atom
183	     counts on both sides.
184	   - exothermic stores a negative delta-energy; endothermic stores positive. *)
185	
186	(* ============================================================
187	   9. Reaction Expressions
188	   ============================================================ *)
189	
190	<reaction_expression> → <reaction_term> { "+" <reaction_term> }
191	
192	<reaction_term> → <species_ref>
193	                | <coefficient> "*" <species_ref>
194	
195	<coefficient> → <number_literal>
196	
197	<species_ref> → <formula_literal> | <identifier>
198	
199	(* Examples accepted:
200	       CH4 + 2*O2        CO2 + 2*H2O
201	       methane + 2*oxygen    co2 + 2*water
202	
203	   In reaction context + separates species and * attaches a coefficient, so
204	   CH4 + 2*O2 parses as CH4 + (2*O2), not (CH4 + 2) * O2.
205	   ANS requires 2*O2 rather than 2O2 to avoid ambiguity with formula subscripts. *)
206	
207	(* ============================================================
208	   10. Expressions
209	   ============================================================ *)
210	
211	<expression> → <comparison_expression>
212	
213	<comparison_expression> → <additive_expression>
214	                          [ ( "==" | "!=" | ">=" | "<=" | ">" | "<" )
215	                            <additive_expression> ]
216	
217	<additive_expression> → <multiplicative_expression>
218	                        { ( "+" | "-" ) <multiplicative_expression> }
219	
220	<multiplicative_expression> → <unary_expression>

(*
ANS Complete EBNF Grammar
Sebesta-style notation for the implemented C-like ANS subset.

Conventions:
  <nonterminal> → production
  terminal      means exact source text (shown in lowercase or quoted)
  { X }         means zero or more repetitions of X
  [ X ]         means optional X
  ( X | Y )     means one of the alternatives X or Y
  |             separates top-level alternatives in a rule
  EOF           means end of file

Important lexer convention:
  ANS uses contextual chemistry words. Lowercase words are first tokenized
  as IDENTIFIER-like words. The parser interprets words such as element,
  compound, reaction, formula, reactants, products, balanced, exothermic,
  and endothermic as special words only in grammar positions where they
  have special meaning. This allows typed parameters such as:

      function compute_yield(reaction r, compound c) { ... };
      function molar_mass(compound c) { ... };
*)

(* ============================================================
   1. Program Structure
   ============================================================ *)

<program> → { <top_level_statement> } EOF

<top_level_statement> → <element_declaration> ";"
                      | <compound_declaration> ";"
                      | <reaction_declaration> ";"
                      | <function_declaration> ";"
                      | <variable_declaration> ";"
                      | <assignment_statement> ";"
                      | <augmented_assignment_statement> ";"
                      | <print_statement> ";"
                      | <expression_statement> ";"
                      | <if_statement>

(* ============================================================
   2. General Statements and Blocks
   ============================================================ *)

<block> → "{" { <statement> } "}"

<statement> → <variable_declaration> ";"
            | <assignment_statement> ";"
            | <augmented_assignment_statement> ";"
            | <return_statement> ";"
            | <print_statement> ";"
            | <expression_statement> ";"
            | <for_statement>
            | <if_statement>

<variable_declaration> → "let" <identifier> "=" <expression>

<assignment_statement> → <assignable> "=" <expression>

<augmented_assignment_statement> → <assignable> <augmented_assignment_operator> <expression>

<augmented_assignment_operator> → "+=" | "-=" | "*=" | "/="

<return_statement> → "return" [ <expression> ]

<print_statement> → "print" <expression>

<expression_statement> → <expression>

(* ============================================================
   3. Function Declarations
   ============================================================ *)

<function_declaration> → "function" <identifier> "(" [ <parameter_list> ] ")" <block>

<parameter_list> → <parameter> { "," <parameter> }

<parameter> → [ <type_name> ] <identifier>

<type_name> → "element" | "compound" | "reaction"

(* Typed parameters allow the type-checker to verify that the correct kind of
   value is passed at call sites. The type annotation is optional; untyped
   parameters accept any value. Examples:
       reaction r    compound c    element e    mol (untyped)

   Ambiguity resolution:
   element, compound, and reaction are parsed as <type_name> only when they
   immediately precede an <identifier> inside a <parameter_list>. Elsewhere
   these words may still appear as identifiers. *)

(* ============================================================
   4. For Loops
   ============================================================ *)

<for_statement> → "for" "(" "let" <identifier> "in" <expression> ")" <block>

(* Example:
   for (let element in formula) {
       mass += element.atomic_mass * formula[element];
   }
*)

(* ============================================================
   5. If / Elif / Else Statements
   ============================================================ *)

<if_statement> → "if" "(" <expression> ")" <block>
                 { <elif_clause> } [ <else_clause> ]

<elif_clause> → "elif" "(" <expression> ")" <block>

<else_clause> → "else" <block>

(* Conditions are always wrapped in parentheses, matching the for-loop style.

   Dangling-else resolution:
   Every branch body is a braced <block>, so the classic unbraced ambiguity
       if a if b s else t
   cannot arise. The optional <else_clause> belongs to the nearest preceding
   <if_statement>. *)

(* ============================================================
   6. Element Declarations
   ============================================================ *)

<element_declaration> → "element" <element_symbol> "{" <element_field_list> "}"

<element_symbol> → <formula_literal>

<element_field_list> → <element_field> { "," <element_field> } [ "," ]

<element_field> → "atomic_mass" "=" <number_literal>
                | "valence"     "=" <number_literal>
                | "symbol"      "=" <string_literal>

(* Semantic requirements:
   - <element_symbol> must be a single valid periodic-table symbol (e.g., H).
   - The element body must contain atomic_mass, valence, and symbol exactly once.
   - Duplicate or missing fields are semantic errors, not syntax errors.
   H is lexically a <formula_literal>; after "element" it is an element symbol. *)

(* ============================================================
   7. Compound Declarations
   ============================================================ *)

<compound_declaration> → "compound" <identifier> "{" <compound_field_list> "}"

<compound_field_list> → <compound_field> { "," <compound_field> } [ "," ]

<compound_field> → "formula" "=" <formula_literal>
                 | "name"    "=" <string_literal>

(* Semantic requirements:
   - The compound body must contain formula and name exactly once.
   - Every element symbol inside <formula_literal> must refer to a declared
     or built-in element. *)

(* ============================================================
   8. Reaction Declarations
   ============================================================ *)

<reaction_declaration> → "reaction" <identifier> "{" <reaction_field_list> "}"

<reaction_field_list> → <reaction_field> { "," <reaction_field> } [ "," ]

<reaction_field> → "reactants" "=" <reaction_expression>
                 | "products"  "=" <reaction_expression>
                 | "check"     "=" <balance_check>
                 | "energy"    "=" <energy_expression>

<balance_check> → "balanced"

<energy_expression> → <energy_kind> <quantity_literal>

<energy_kind> → "exothermic" | "endothermic"

(* Semantic requirements:
   - The reaction body must contain reactants, products, check, and energy
     exactly once.
   - If check = balanced appears, the semantic checker verifies equal atom
     counts on both sides.
   - exothermic stores a negative delta-energy; endothermic stores positive. *)

(* ============================================================
   9. Reaction Expressions
   ============================================================ *)

<reaction_expression> → <reaction_term> { "+" <reaction_term> }

<reaction_term> → <species_ref>
                | <coefficient> "*" <species_ref>

<coefficient> → <number_literal>

<species_ref> → <formula_literal> | <identifier>

(* Examples accepted:
       CH4 + 2*O2        CO2 + 2*H2O
       methane + 2*oxygen    co2 + 2*water

   In reaction context + separates species and * attaches a coefficient, so
   CH4 + 2*O2 parses as CH4 + (2*O2), not (CH4 + 2) * O2.
   ANS requires 2*O2 rather than 2O2 to avoid ambiguity with formula subscripts. *)

(* ============================================================
   10. Expressions
   ============================================================ *)

<expression> → <comparison_expression>

<comparison_expression> → <additive_expression>
                          [ ( "==" | "!=" | ">=" | "<=" | ">" | "<" )
                            <additive_expression> ]

<additive_expression> → <multiplicative_expression>
                        { ( "+" | "-" ) <multiplicative_expression> }

<multiplicative_expression> → <unary_expression>
                               { ( "*" | "/" ) <unary_expression> }

<unary_expression> → [ "-" ] <postfix_expression>

<postfix_expression> → <primary_expression> { <postfix_operator> }

<postfix_operator> → "." <identifier>
                   | "[" <expression> "]"
                   | "(" [ <argument_list> ] ")"

<primary_expression> → <number_or_quantity_literal>
                     | <string_literal>
                     | <char_literal>
                     | <list_literal>
                     | <formula_literal>
                     | <identifier>
                     | "(" <expression> ")"

<argument_list> → <expression> { "," <expression> }

<number_or_quantity_literal> → <number_literal> [ <unit> ]

<quantity_literal> → <number_literal> <unit>

<unit> → UNIT_LITERAL | "mol" | "g" | "kg" | "kJ"

(* Notation note: the quoted alternatives "mol", "g", "kg", "kJ" match an
   IDENTIFIER token whose lexeme equals that string — they are not a separate
   token class. The lexer emits IDENTIFIER in all four cases; the parser
   accepts the token here by lexeme value, exactly as it does for contextual
   keywords such as "balanced" and "exothermic".

   Unit design (Option C):
   UNIT_LITERAL covers only the three slash-compound forms: g/mol, kg/mol,
   kJ/mol. These contain "/" and can never be valid identifiers, so the lexer
   recognises them by priority over the operator "/" — a straightforward
   longest-match rule, not context-sensitive.

   Single-word units mol, g, kg, kJ are always emitted as IDENTIFIER tokens
   by the pure FA scanner. The parser promotes them to <unit> only when they
   directly follow a <number_literal> inside <number_or_quantity_literal> or
   <quantity_literal>. Everywhere else (function parameters, property names,
   expressions) the same tokens remain plain identifiers. No lexer statefulness
   is required. *)

<list_literal> → "[" [ <argument_list> ] "]"

(* Operator precedence (lowest to highest):
   1. comparison:     == != >= <= > <
   2. additive:       + -
   3. multiplicative: * /
   4. unary:          -
   5. postfix:        call ( ), index [ ], property .
   6. primary:        literals, identifiers, ( <expression> )
   Binary +, -, *, / are left-associative (left-to-right repetition in grammar). *)

(* ============================================================
   11. Assignable Expressions
   ============================================================ *)

<assignable> → <identifier> { <assignable_postfix> }

<assignable_postfix> → "." <identifier>
                     | "[" <expression> "]"

(* Function-call syntax is excluded from <assignable>, so f(x) = 3 is invalid. *)

(* ============================================================
   12. Lexical Nonterminals
   ============================================================ *)

<identifier>      → IDENTIFIER
<number_literal>  → NUMBER_LITERAL
<string_literal>  → STRING_LITERAL
<char_literal>    → CHAR_LITERAL
<formula_literal> → FORMULA_LITERAL

(* Lexer patterns:

   IDENTIFIER:
       [a-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*

   NUMBER_LITERAL:
       (?:0|[1-9][0-9]*)(?:\.[0-9]+)?(?:[eE][+-]?[0-9]+)?

   STRING_LITERAL:
       "(?:[^"\\\r\n]|\\["\\nrt])*"

   CHAR_LITERAL:
       '(?:[^'\\\r\n]|\\['\\nrt])'

   FORMULA_LITERAL:
       (?:[A-Z][a-z]?(?:[1-9][0-9]*)?)+

   UNIT_LITERAL:
       kg/mol|g/mol|kJ/mol
       (slash-compound units only; tried before IDENTIFIER by lexer priority)

   OPERATOR:
       ==|!=|>=|<=|\+=|-=|\*=|/=|=|[+\-*/><]

   SEPARATOR:
       [{}()\[\],;.]

   COMMENT:
       //[^\r\n]*

   WHITESPACE:
       [ \t\f\r\n]+
*)

(* ============================================================
   13. Contextual Keyword and Unit Resolution
   ============================================================ *)

(* Hard reserved words:
     let  function  return  for  in  if  elif  else  print

   Contextual declaration/chemistry words:
     element  compound  reaction  atomic_mass  valence  symbol  formula
     name  reactants  products  check  balanced  energy  exothermic  endothermic

   Compound unit tokens (UNIT_LITERAL, lexer level):
     g/mol  kg/mol  kJ/mol

   Single-word unit identifiers (parser level):
     mol  g  kg  kJ
     These are always emitted as IDENTIFIER by the scanner.
     The parser recognises them as <unit> only when they follow a
     <number_literal> inside <number_or_quantity_literal> or <quantity_literal>.

   Resolution rules:
   - At declaration start, element/compound/reaction are declaration keywords.
   - Inside declaration bodies, field-name words are field identifiers.
   - Immediately before an <identifier> inside <parameter_list>, element,
     compound, and reaction are parsed as <type_name> annotations.
   - In expression and property positions the same words are identifiers. *)

(* ============================================================
   14. Ambiguity Summary
   ============================================================ *)

(*
1. Operator precedence:
   Resolved by separate comparison, additive, multiplicative, unary, postfix,
   and primary expression levels.

2. Reaction precedence:
   Resolved by a separate <reaction_expression> grammar.

3. Stoichiometric coefficient ambiguity:
   Resolved by requiring 2*O2 instead of 2O2.

4. Formula versus identifier ambiguity:
   Identifiers start with a lowercase letter or _; formula literals start with
   an uppercase letter. water is an identifier; H2O is a formula literal.

5. Compound-name species versus formula species:
   Resolved by <species_ref>, which accepts either form inside reactions.

6. Keyword versus identifier ambiguity:
   Resolved with contextual keywords. element, compound, and reaction act as
   type annotations in parameter lists; everywhere else they are identifiers.

7. Unit versus identifier ambiguity:
   Compound units g/mol, kg/mol, kJ/mol are UNIT_LITERAL tokens (lexer level,
   priority over "/"). Single-word units mol, g, kg, kJ are always IDENTIFIER

   literal in <number_or_quantity_literal> or <quantity_literal>.

1	# 4.6 Names, Binding, Scope, and Lifetime
2	
3	*Citing Sebesta Ch. 5*
4	
5	---
6	
7	## Legal Identifiers (Sebesta §5.1)
8	
9	An ANS identifier must match the pattern `[a-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`: it begins with a lowercase letter or underscore and continues with any mix of letters, digits, and underscores. ANS is **case-sensitive**, so `water` and `Water` are entirely different tokens — and in fact `Water` is not a legal identifier at all, because any token beginning with an uppercase letter is classified as a `FORMULA_LITERAL` by the lexer (`H`, `O2`, `H2O`). This case split is a deliberate design choice: chemistry notation and program names are kept visually separate with no additional keyword rules.
10	
11	**Hard reserved words** — may never be used as identifiers:
12	
13	```
14	let  function  return  for  in  if  elif  else  print
15	```
16	
17	**Contextual keywords** — reserved only in specific grammar positions; valid identifiers everywhere else:
18	
19	```
20	element  compound  reaction
21	atomic_mass  valence  symbol  formula  name
22	reactants  products  check  balanced  energy  exothermic  endothermic
23	```
24	
25	This means `function compute_yield(reaction r, compound c)` is legal: `reaction` and `compound` act as type annotations inside the parameter list, but the same words are plain identifiers in expressions. A name may not be declared twice in the same scope. An inner-scope `let` may shadow an outer binding — for example, `let formula = c.formula` inside `molar_mass` shadows the contextual field keyword `formula` — a warning for this will be emitted by the semantic checker in Part 2.
26	
27	---
28	
29	## Bindings: Compile Time vs. Run Time (Sebesta §5.2)
30	
31	| Binding | When | Example from `main.ans` |
32	|---|---|---|
33	| Operator symbol → semantics | Language-design time | `+`, `*`, `==`, `+=` |
34	| Lexeme → token category | Lex / compile time | `water` → `IDENTIFIER`, `H2O` → `FORMULA_LITERAL` |
35	| Identifier → declaration | Compile time (static scope walk) | `mass` in `molar_mass` resolves to its `let` declaration |
36	| Variable → inferred type | Compile time | `let n = 21.2` → Float; `let name = "Hydrogen"` → String |
37	| Parameter → declared type | Compile time | `compound c` in `molar_mass` fixes `c` as Compound |
38	| Element / compound / reaction → declaration | Compile time | `water`, `combustion` resolved before execution |
39	| Formula validity | Compile time | every symbol in `H2O` must name a declared element |
40	| `check = balanced` | Compile time | atom counts on both sides verified statically |
41	| `mol` → built-in function declaration | Compile time | pre-declared; resolved before any user code is checked |
42	| Parameter → argument value | Run time (call) | `molar_mass(water)` binds `c` to the `water` object |
43	| Local variable → storage cell | Run time (block entry) | `let mass = 0.0` allocates on function entry |
44	| Variable → value | Run time (assignment) | `mass += element.atomic_mass * formula[element]` |
45	| Loop variable → current element | Run time (each iteration) | `let element in formula` rebinds each step |
46	| Function call → return value | Run time | `return mass` passes the computed float back |
47	
48	ANS maximises **compile-time bindings** by design: type inference, formula validation, and balance checking all happen before execution, catching chemistry errors as early as possible.
49	
50	---
51	
52	## Static Scoping vs. Dynamic Scoping (Sebesta §5.5)
53	
54	ANS uses **static (lexical) scoping**. Every name resolves to the nearest enclosing declaration in the *source text*: the current block, then each successively enclosing block, up to the top-level program scope.
55	
56	### Why static scoping?
57	
58	Because ANS performs compile-time formula validation and balance checking, the compiler must be able to determine which compound or reaction a name refers to from the source text alone — without simulating execution. Static scoping makes this possible. It also makes programs easier to read: the meaning of every name can be found by looking upward in the source without knowing the call history.
59	
60	### What would break under dynamic scoping?
61	
62	Consider this pair of functions from `main.ans`:
63	
64	```ans
65	function molar_mass(compound c) {
66	    let formula = c.formula;
67	    let mass = 0.0;
68	    for (let element in formula) {
69	        mass += element.atomic_mass * formula[element];
70	    }
71	    return mass;
72	};
73	
74	function compute_yield(reaction r, compound c) {
75	    let products = r.products;
76	    let reactants = r.reactants;
77	    let reactant_mol = 1.0 / mol(reactants[c]);
78	    let product_mol = reactant_mol * mol(products[c]);
79	    return product_mol;
80	};
81	```
82	
83	Under **dynamic scoping**, `formula` inside `molar_mass` would not refer to the local `let formula = c.formula` but to whatever binding of `formula` happened to exist in the caller's scope at the moment of the call. If `compute_yield` called `molar_mass` and the caller had its own `let formula = ...`, the calculation would silently use the wrong data. More critically, `element` in the `for` loop would capture any `element` variable visible in the call chain, potentially iterating over a chemistry declaration object rather than a formula map. The compile-time balance check on `reaction combustion` depends on statically resolving `CH4`, `O2`, `CO2`, and `H2O` to their declared compounds; under dynamic scoping that resolution would be deferred to run time, making static verification impossible.
84	
85	---
86

# 4.6 Names, Binding, Scope, and Lifetime

*Citing Sebesta Ch. 5*

---

## Legal Identifiers (Sebesta §5.1)

An ANS identifier must match the pattern `[a-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`: it begins with a lowercase letter or underscore and continues with any mix of letters, digits, and underscores. ANS is **case-sensitive**, so `water` and `Water` are entirely different tokens — and in fact `Water` is not a legal identifier at all, because any token beginning with an uppercase letter is classified as a `FORMULA_LITERAL` by the lexer (`H`, `O2`, `H2O`). This case split is a deliberate design choice: chemistry notation and program names are kept visually separate with no additional keyword rules.

**Hard reserved words** — may never be used as identifiers:

```
let  function  return  for  in  if  elif  else  print
```

**Contextual keywords** — reserved only in specific grammar positions; valid identifiers everywhere else:

```
element  compound  reaction
atomic_mass  valence  symbol  formula  name
reactants  products  check  balanced  energy  exothermic  endothermic
```

This means `function compute_yield(reaction r, compound c)` is legal: `reaction` and `compound` act as type annotations inside the parameter list, but the same words are plain identifiers in expressions. A name may not be declared twice in the same scope. An inner-scope `let` may shadow an outer binding — for example, `let formula = c.formula` inside `molar_mass` shadows the contextual field keyword `formula` — a warning for this will be emitted by the semantic checker in Part 2.

---

## Bindings: Compile Time vs. Run Time (Sebesta §5.2)

| Binding | When | Example from `main.ans` |
|---|---|---|
| Operator symbol → semantics | Language-design time | `+`, `*`, `==`, `+=` |
| Lexeme → token category | Lex / compile time | `water` → `IDENTIFIER`, `H2O` → `FORMULA_LITERAL` |
| Identifier → declaration | Compile time (static scope walk) | `mass` in `molar_mass` resolves to its `let` declaration |
| Variable → inferred type | Compile time | `let n = 21.2` → Float; `let name = "Hydrogen"` → String |
| Parameter → declared type | Compile time | `compound c` in `molar_mass` fixes `c` as Compound |
| Element / compound / reaction → declaration | Compile time | `water`, `combustion` resolved before execution |
| Formula validity | Compile time | every symbol in `H2O` must name a declared element |
| `check = balanced` | Compile time | atom counts on both sides verified statically |
| `mol` → built-in function declaration | Compile time | pre-declared; resolved before any user code is checked |
| Parameter → argument value | Run time (call) | `molar_mass(water)` binds `c` to the `water` object |
| Local variable → storage cell | Run time (block entry) | `let mass = 0.0` allocates on function entry |
| Variable → value | Run time (assignment) | `mass += element.atomic_mass * formula[element]` |
| Loop variable → current element | Run time (each iteration) | `let element in formula` rebinds each step |
| Function call → return value | Run time | `return mass` passes the computed float back |

ANS maximises **compile-time bindings** by design: type inference, formula validation, and balance checking all happen before execution, catching chemistry errors as early as possible.

---

## Static Scoping vs. Dynamic Scoping (Sebesta §5.5)

ANS uses **static (lexical) scoping**. Every name resolves to the nearest enclosing declaration in the *source text*: the current block, then each successively enclosing block, up to the top-level program scope.

### Why static scoping?

Because ANS performs compile-time formula validation and balance checking, the compiler must be able to determine which compound or reaction a name refers to from the source text alone — without simulating execution. Static scoping makes this possible. It also makes programs easier to read: the meaning of every name can be found by looking upward in the source without knowing the call history.

### What would break under dynamic scoping?

Consider this pair of functions from `main.ans`:

```ans
function molar_mass(compound c) {
    let formula = c.formula;
    let mass = 0.0;
    for (let element in formula) {
        mass += element.atomic_mass * formula[element];
    }
    return mass;
};

function compute_yield(reaction r, compound c) {
    let products = r.products;
    let reactants = r.reactants;
    let reactant_mol = 1.0 / mol(reactants[c]);
    let product_mol = reactant_mol * mol(products[c]);
    return product_mol;
};
```

Under **dynamic scoping**, `formula` inside `molar_mass` would not refer to the local `let formula = c.formula` but to whatever binding of `formula` happened to exist in the caller's scope at the moment of the call. If `compute_yield` called `molar_mass` and the caller had its own `let formula = ...`, the calculation would silently use the wrong data. More critically, `element` in the `for` loop would capture any `element` variable visible in the call chain, potentially iterating over a chemistry declaration object rather than a formula map. The compile-time balance check on `reaction combustion` depends on statically resolving `CH4`, `O2`, `CO2`, and `H2O` to their declared compounds; under dynamic scoping that resolution would be deferred to run time, making static verification impossible.

---

## Lifetime of Variables (Sebesta §5.4.3)

| Entity | Lifetime | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `element H { ... }`, `element O { ... }`, `element C { ... }` | **Static** | Allocated once at program start; visible to every subsequent statement and function |
| `compound water { ... }`, `compound methane { ... }`, etc. | **Static** | Same as element declarations |
| `reaction combustion { ... }`, `reaction combustion2 { ... }` | **Static** | Verified at compile time; exists for the program's entire lifetime |
| Top-level `let num`, `let name`, `let elements`, `let list`, etc. | **Static** | Single binding from declaration to program termination |
| Function parameters (`reaction r`, `compound c`) | **Stack-dynamic** | Allocated on each call to `compute_yield` or `molar_mass`; deallocated on return. Supports recursion. |
| Local `let` inside a function (`let formula`, `let mass`, `let products`) | **Stack-dynamic** | Allocated when the declaration is reached during execution; freed when the enclosing block exits |
| `for` loop variable (`let element in formula`) | **Stack-dynamic** | Bound at the start of the `for` block and freed when the `for` block exits — one allocation for the entire loop, rebound to the next element each iteration |
| `mol` (built-in function) | **Static** | Pre-declared before program execution; always visible |
| List values, compound objects, reaction objects | **Implicit heap-dynamic** (Sebesta §5.4.3) | Managed internally by the runtime — not *explicit*-heap-dynamic in Sebesta's sense, because ANS exposes no `new`, no `delete`, and no pointers |

ANS deliberately has **no explicit-heap-dynamic storage**. There are no pointers, no `new`/`delete`, and no aliasing. This eliminates an entire class of reliability errors (use-after-free, double-free, dangling pointers) — a direct consequence of prioritising reliability over flexibility, as stated in §4.1.

# ANS — Alchemist's Notation Script

ANS is a domain-specific language for declaring chemical elements, compounds, and reactions, verifying atomic balance at compile time, and performing stoichiometric queries such as molar mass and theoretical yield. It is designed so that programs read the way chemistry appears in textbooks rather than as bare numerical code.

Developed as the term project for **CSE 341 — Concepts of Programming Languages** at Gebze Technical University, Spring 2026.

**Authors:** Yusuf Hamza Çelebi (220104004926) · Enes Özkan (220104004931)

---

## Table of Contents

1. [Design Goals](#design-goals)
2. [Quick Example](#quick-example)
3. [Language Reference](#language-reference)
   - [Declarations](#declarations)
   - [Variables](#variables)
   - [Functions](#functions)
   - [Control Flow](#control-flow)
   - [Expressions](#expressions)
   - [Literals](#literals)
4. [Lexical Structure](#lexical-structure)
5. [Grammar (EBNF Summary)](#grammar-ebnf-summary)
6. [Names, Scoping, and Lifetime](#names-scoping-and-lifetime)
7. [Implementation](#implementation)
8. [Build & Run](#build--run)
9. [Error Reporting](#error-reporting)
10. [Test Suite](#test-suite)
11. [Project Layout](#project-layout)

---

## Design Goals

ANS applies Sebesta's four evaluation criteria (Ch. 1) as follows:

| Criterion | Decision |
|---|---|
| **Readability** | Syntax mirrors chemistry vocabulary directly — `element`, `compound`, `reaction`, `reactants`, `products`, `balanced` — over a familiar C-like skeleton (`let`, braces, semicolons, `if`/`elif`/`else`). |
| **Writability** | Common domain tasks are first-class constructs: declaring an element, writing a balanced equation as `CH4 + 2*O2`, querying `molar_mass(water)`. No boilerplate library imports required. |
| **Reliability** | Formula literals (`H2O`, `CH4`) and unit literals (`mol`, `kJ/mol`) are distinct token categories. `check = balanced` reactions are verified for atomic equality at compile time. |
| **Cost / Trade-offs** | Higher implementation cost for formula parsing, unit handling, and balance checking. Reduced generality (unsuited to non-chemistry tasks) and reduced orthogonality (fixed domain forms replace freely-combinable primitives). |

---

## Quick Example

```ans
// Declare elements
element H { atomic_mass = 1.008, valence = 1, symbol = "H" };
element O { atomic_mass = 15.999, valence = 2, symbol = "O" };
element C { atomic_mass = 12.011, valence = 4, symbol = "C" };

// Declare compounds
compound water   { formula = H2O, name = "Water" };
compound methane { formula = CH4, name = "Methane" };
compound co2     { formula = CO2, name = "Carbon dioxide" };
compound oxygen  { formula = O2,  name = "Oxygen" };

// Declare a reaction and verify it is balanced at compile time
reaction combustion {
    reactants = CH4 + 2*O2,
    products  = CO2 + 2*H2O,
    check     = balanced,
    energy    = exothermic 890.3 kJ/mol
};

// Function using typed parameters
function molar_mass(compound c) {
    let formula = c.formula;
    let mass = 0.0;
    for (let element in formula) {
        mass += element.atomic_mass * formula[element];
    }
    return mass;
};

// Stoichiometric queries
molar_mass(water);

if (molar_mass(water) > 18.0) {
    print "Heavier than expected.";
}
elif (molar_mass(water) == 18.0) {
    print "Exactly 18 g/mol.";
}
else {
    print "Lighter than expected.";
}
```

---

## Language Reference

### Declarations

All declarations live at the top level and are terminated with `;`.

#### `element`

Declares a chemical element. The name must be a **formula literal** (uppercase-leading, e.g. `H`, `O`, `Na`).

```ans
element H {
    atomic_mass = 1.008,
    valence     = 1,
    symbol      = "H"
};
```

Required fields: `atomic_mass` (number), `valence` (number), `symbol` (string). Order is flexible; a trailing comma is allowed.

#### `compound`

Declares a named chemical compound. The identifier is a lowercase program name; `formula` holds the chemical formula as a formula literal.

```ans
compound water {
    formula = H2O,
    name    = "Water"
};
```

Required fields: `formula` (formula literal), `name` (string).

#### `reaction`

Declares a chemical reaction. Species in `reactants` and `products` may be formula literals (`CH4`, `O2`) or compound identifiers (`methane`, `water`). Stoichiometric coefficients are written `2*O2` — the `*` is required to distinguish coefficients from formula subscripts.

```ans
reaction combustion {
    reactants = CH4 + 2*O2,
    products  = CO2 + 2*H2O,
    check     = balanced,
    energy    = exothermic 890.3 kJ/mol
};
```

Fields:
- `reactants` / `products` — reaction expressions
- `check = balanced` — requests compile-time atom-count verification
- `energy = exothermic <qty>` or `energy = endothermic <qty>` — energy annotation

### Variables

```ans
let x = 42;
let name = "Hydrogen";
let ch = 'H';
let items = [H, O, C];
let n = 6.02e23;
```

Variables are declared with `let`. Types are inferred at compile time. Augmented assignment operators `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=` are supported.

### Functions

```ans
// Typed parameters
function molar_mass(compound c) {
    let mass = 0.0;
    return mass;
};

// Untyped parameter
function double_val(x) {
    return x * 2.0;
};

// No parameters
function get_avogadro() {
    return 6.02e23;
};
```

- Parameters may optionally carry a type annotation: `element`, `compound`, or `reaction`.
- Untyped parameters accept any value.
- `return` with no expression returns from a void function.

### Control Flow

#### `for` — iterator loop

```ans
for (let element in formula) {
    mass += element.atomic_mass * formula[element];
}
```

#### `if` / `elif` / `else`

```ans
if (mass > 18.0) {
    print "Heavy.";
}
elif (mass == 18.0) {
    print "Exactly 18.";
}
else {
    print "Light.";
}
```

All branch bodies are braced blocks — there is no dangling-else ambiguity.

#### `print`

```ans
print "The yield is positive.";
print molar_mass(water);
```

### Expressions

Operator precedence (lowest to highest):

| Level | Operators |
|---|---|
| Comparison | `==` `!=` `>=` `<=` `>` `<` |
| Additive | `+` `-` |
| Multiplicative | `*` `/` |
| Unary | `-` |
| Postfix | call `()`, index `[]`, member `.` |
| Primary | literals, identifiers, `(expr)` |

Binary `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` are left-associative. A single comparison is allowed per expression (no chaining).

Member access and indexing:

```ans
c.formula          // property access
formula[element]   // index access
molar_mass(water)  // function call
```

### Literals

| Kind | Examples |
|---|---|
| Number | `20`, `1.008`, `21.2`, `890.3`, `6.02e23` |
| String | `"Water"`, `"Carbon dioxide"` |
| Character | `'H'`, `'\n'` |
| Formula | `H`, `O2`, `H2O`, `CH4`, `CO2` |
| Quantity | `5.0 mol`, `890.3 kJ/mol`, `18.0 g/mol` |
| List | `[H, O, C]`, `[1, "two", 3.45]` |

---

## Lexical Structure

ANS uses six token categories produced by a maximal-munch (longest-match) scanner followed by a reserved-word filter.

### Identifiers

```
[a-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*
```

User-defined names always start with a lowercase letter or `_`. Any token starting with an uppercase letter is classified as a **formula literal**, not an identifier — this is how `water` and `H2O` are kept visually and grammatically separate without extra keyword rules.

### Formula Literals

```
([A-Z][a-z]?[0-9]*)+
```

Examples: `H`, `O`, `Na`, `H2O`, `CH4`, `CO2`, `NaCl`. The lexer produces a single `FORMULA` token for a whole molecular formula; no lookahead or statefulness is required.

### Unit Literals

Compound units containing `/` are scanned as a single token before the `/` operator is considered:

```
kg/mol | g/mol | kJ/mol
```

Single-word units (`mol`, `g`, `kg`, `kJ`) are emitted as identifiers by the scanner and promoted to `<unit>` role by the parser only when they immediately follow a number literal.

### Keywords

**Hard reserved words** (may never be used as identifiers):

```
let  function  return  for  in  if  elif  else  print
```

**Contextual keywords** (valid identifiers in all other positions; promoted by the parser based on grammar context):

| Position | Words |
|---|---|
| Declaration head | `element` `compound` `reaction` |
| Declaration field names | `atomic_mass` `valence` `symbol` `formula` `name` `reactants` `products` `check` `energy` |
| Reaction field values | `balanced` `exothermic` `endothermic` |
| Parameter type annotations | `element` `compound` `reaction` |

### Operators

```
==  !=  <=  >=  +=  -=  *=  /=  =  +  -  *  /  <  >
```

### Separators

```
{  }  (  )  [  ]  ,  ;  .
```

### Comments

Line comments only, discarded before parsing:

```
// This is a comment
```

---

## Grammar (EBNF Summary)

```ebnf
<program>             → { <top_level_statement> } EOF

<top_level_statement> → <element_declaration> ";"
                      | <compound_declaration> ";"
                      | <reaction_declaration> ";"
                      | <function_declaration> ";"
                      | <variable_declaration> ";"
                      | <print_statement> ";"
                      | <expression_statement> ";"
                      | <if_statement>
                      | <for_statement>

<element_declaration> → "element" <formula_literal> "{" <element_field_list> "}"
<element_field>       → "atomic_mass" "=" <number_literal>
                      | "valence"     "=" <number_literal>
                      | "symbol"      "=" <string_literal>

<compound_declaration>→ "compound" <identifier> "{" <compound_field_list> "}"
<compound_field>      → "formula" "=" <formula_literal>
                      | "name"    "=" <string_literal>

<reaction_declaration>→ "reaction" <identifier> "{" <reaction_field_list> "}"
<reaction_field>      → "reactants" "=" <reaction_expression>
                      | "products"  "=" <reaction_expression>
                      | "check"     "=" "balanced"
                      | "energy"    "=" ( "exothermic" | "endothermic" ) <quantity_literal>

<reaction_expression> → <reaction_term> { "+" <reaction_term> }
<reaction_term>       → <species_ref> | <number_literal> "*" <species_ref>
<species_ref>         → <formula_literal> | <identifier>

<function_declaration>→ "function" <identifier> "(" [ <parameter_list> ] ")" <block>
<parameter>           → [ <type_name> ] <identifier>
<type_name>           → "element" | "compound" | "reaction"

<for_statement>       → "for" "(" "let" <identifier> "in" <expression> ")" <block>
<if_statement>        → "if" "(" <expression> ")" <block>
                        { "elif" "(" <expression> ")" <block> }
                        [ "else" <block> ]

<expression>          → <comparison_expression>
<comparison_expression> → <additive_expression>
                          [ ( "==" | "!=" | ">=" | "<=" | ">" | "<" ) <additive_expression> ]
<additive_expression> → <multiplicative_expression> { ( "+" | "-" ) <multiplicative_expression> }
<multiplicative_expression> → <unary_expression> { ( "*" | "/" ) <unary_expression> }
<unary_expression>    → [ "-" ] <postfix_expression>
<postfix_expression>  → <primary_expression> { "." <identifier> | "[" <expression> "]" | "(" [ <argument_list> ] ")" }
<primary_expression>  → <number_or_quantity_literal> | <string_literal> | <char_literal>
                      | <formula_literal> | <list_literal> | <identifier>
                      | "(" <expression> ")"

<number_or_quantity_literal> → <number_literal> [ <unit> ]
<unit>                → UNIT_LITERAL | "mol" | "g" | "kg" | "kJ"
<list_literal>        → "[" [ <argument_list> ] "]"
```

The full EBNF is in `D1/4.3/EBNF/ANS_complete_EBNF.ebnf`.

---

## Names, Scoping, and Lifetime

**Case sensitivity.** ANS is fully case-sensitive. Tokens starting with uppercase are always formula literals; lowercase-starting tokens are identifiers. There is no ambiguity.

**Static (lexical) scoping.** Every name resolves to the nearest enclosing declaration in the source text, outward to the top-level program scope. This is required for compile-time formula validation and balance checking — the compiler must resolve names from source text alone without simulating execution.

**Compile-time vs. run-time bindings:**

| Binding | When |
|---|---|
| Operator symbol → semantics | Language-design time |
| Lexeme → token category | Compile time (lex) |
| Identifier → declaration | Compile time (static scope walk) |
| Variable → inferred type | Compile time |
| Parameter → declared type | Compile time |
| Formula validity | Compile time |
| `check = balanced` | Compile time |
| Parameter → argument value | Run time (call) |
| Local variable → storage cell | Run time (block entry) |
| Loop variable → current element | Run time (each iteration) |

**Storage lifetimes:**

| Entity | Lifetime |
|---|---|
| `element`, `compound`, `reaction` declarations | Static — allocated once, live for the whole program |
| Top-level `let` variables | Static |
| Function parameters | Stack-dynamic — allocated per call, supports recursion |
| Local `let` inside a function/block | Stack-dynamic — freed on block exit |
| `for` loop variable | Stack-dynamic — one allocation for the loop, rebound each iteration |
| List/compound/reaction values | Implicit heap-dynamic (runtime-managed, no explicit `new`/`delete`) |

ANS has **no explicit-heap-dynamic storage**, no pointers, and no aliasing, eliminating use-after-free and dangling-pointer errors by design.

---

## Implementation

The current implementation is a hand-written C11 front end (lexer + parser + AST) in `D2/`.

### Components

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `src/lexer.c` | Maximal-munch scanner: whitespace/comment skipping, formula/unit/keyword scanning |
| `src/parser.c` | Recursive-descent parser — one function per EBNF rule |
| `src/ast.c` | AST node constructors and tree pretty-printer |
| `src/error.c` | `<file>:<line>:<col>: error:` formatting |
| `src/main.c` | CLI entry point: reads file, runs lexer + parser, optionally dumps AST |

### Parser strategy

The parser is a single-token lookahead recursive-descent parser matching the EBNF grammar exactly. Panic-mode error recovery skips to the next `;`, `}`, or EOF on any syntax error, allowing multiple errors to be reported per run.

**Contextual keyword disambiguation** happens entirely in the parser: `element`, `compound`, and `reaction` are contextual, resolved as declaration keywords vs. type annotations based on grammar position. The lexer emits plain `IDENT` for all three.

**Formula vs. identifier disambiguation** is done in the lexer by case: uppercase-leading → `FORMULA`, lowercase/`_`-leading → `IDENT`.

**Unit disambiguation**: compound units (`g/mol`, `kg/mol`, `kJ/mol`) are probed before consuming `/`, so they are emitted as `UNIT_LIT` without lexer statefulness. Single-word units (`mol`, `g`, `kg`, `kJ`) are always `IDENT`; the parser recognises them as `<unit>` only when they follow a number.

---

## Build & Run

Requires a C11 compiler (`cc`). No external dependencies.

```sh
cd D2

make          # optimised build → ./ans
make debug    # add -g -DDEBUG
make clean
```

```sh
./ans <file.ans>                # parse; exit 0 on success, 1 on error
./ans --dump-ast <file.ans>     # parse and print the AST to stdout
```

### AST dump example

```
$ ./ans --dump-ast tests/valid/elements.ans
Program
├── ElementDecl [H]
│   ├── ElementField [atomic_mass]
│   │   └── Number [1.008]
│   ├── ElementField [valence]
│   │   └── Number [1]
│   └── ElementField [symbol]

# ANS — Alchemist's Notation Script

ANS is a domain-specific language for declaring chemical elements, compounds, and reactions, verifying atomic balance at compile time, and performing stoichiometric queries such as molar mass and theoretical yield. It is designed so that programs read the way chemistry appears in textbooks rather than as bare numerical code.

Developed as the term project for **CSE 341 — Concepts of Programming Languages** at Gebze Technical University, Spring 2026.

**Authors:** Yusuf Hamza Çelebi (220104004926) · Enes Özkan (220104004931)

---

2. [Quick Example](#quick-example)

---

## Design Goals

ANS applies Sebesta's four evaluation criteria (Ch. 1) as follows:

| Criterion | Decision |
|---|---|
| **Readability** | Syntax mirrors chemistry vocabulary directly — `element`, `compound`, `reaction`, `reactants`, `products`, `balanced` — over a familiar C-like skeleton (`let`, braces, semicolons, `if`/`elif`/`else`). |
| **Writability** | Common domain tasks are first-class constructs: declaring an element, writing a balanced equation as `CH4 + 2*O2`, querying `molar_mass(water)`. No boilerplate library imports required. |
| **Reliability** | Formula literals (`H2O`, `CH4`) and unit literals (`mol`, `kJ/mol`) are distinct token categories. `check = balanced` reactions are verified for atomic equality at compile time. |
| **Cost / Trade-offs** | Higher implementation cost for formula parsing, unit handling, and balance checking. Reduced generality (unsuited to non-chemistry tasks) and reduced orthogonality (fixed domain forms replace freely-combinable primitives). |

---

## Quick Example

```ans
// Declare elements
element H { atomic_mass = 1.008, valence = 1, symbol = "H" };
element O { atomic_mass = 15.999, valence = 2, symbol = "O" };
element C { atomic_mass = 12.011, valence = 4, symbol = "C" };

// Declare compounds
compound water   { formula = H2O, name = "Water" };
compound methane { formula = CH4, name = "Methane" };
compound co2     { formula = CO2, name = "Carbon dioxide" };
compound oxygen  { formula = O2,  name = "Oxygen" };

// Declare a reaction and verify it is balanced at compile time
reaction combustion {
    reactants = CH4 + 2*O2,
    products  = CO2 + 2*H2O,
    check     = balanced,
    energy    = exothermic 890.3 kJ/mol
};

// Function using typed parameters
function molar_mass(compound c) {
    let formula = c.formula;
    let mass = 0.0;
    for (let element in formula) {
        mass += element.atomic_mass * formula[element];
    }
    return mass;
};

// Stoichiometric queries
molar_mass(water);

if (molar_mass(water) > 18.0) {
    print "Heavier than expected.";
}
elif (molar_mass(water) == 18.0) {
    print "Exactly 18 g/mol.";
}
else {
    print "Lighter than expected.";
}
```

---

## Language Reference

### Declarations

All declarations live at the top level and are terminated with `;`.

#### `element`

Declares a chemical element. The name must be a **formula literal** (uppercase-leading, e.g. `H`, `O`, `Na`).

```ans
element H {
    atomic_mass = 1.008,
    valence     = 1,
    symbol      = "H"
};
```

Required fields: `atomic_mass` (number), `valence` (number), `symbol` (string). Order is flexible; a trailing comma is allowed.

#### `compound`

Declares a named chemical compound. The identifier is a lowercase program name; `formula` holds the chemical formula as a formula literal.

```ans
compound water {
    formula = H2O,
    name    = "Water"
};
```

Required fields: `formula` (formula literal), `name` (string).

#### `reaction`

Declares a chemical reaction. Species in `reactants` and `products` may be formula literals (`CH4`, `O2`) or compound identifiers (`methane`, `water`). Stoichiometric coefficients are written `2*O2` — the `*` is required to distinguish coefficients from formula subscripts.

```ans
reaction combustion {
    reactants = CH4 + 2*O2,
    products  = CO2 + 2*H2O,
    check     = balanced,
    energy    = exothermic 890.3 kJ/mol
};
```

Fields:
- `reactants` / `products` — reaction expressions
- `check = balanced` — requests compile-time atom-count verification
- `energy = exothermic <qty>` or `energy = endothermic <qty>` — energy annotation

### Variables

```ans
let x = 42;
let name = "Hydrogen";
let ch = 'H';
let items = [H, O, C];
let n = 6.02e23;
```

Variables are declared with `let`. Types are inferred at compile time. Augmented assignment operators `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=` are supported.

### Functions

```ans
// Typed parameters
function molar_mass(compound c) {
    let mass = 0.0;
    return mass;
};

// Untyped parameter
function double_val(x) {
    return x * 2.0;
};

// No parameters
function get_avogadro() {
    return 6.02e23;
};
```

- Parameters may optionally carry a type annotation: `element`, `compound`, or `reaction`.
- Untyped parameters accept any value.
- `return` with no expression returns from a void function.

### Control Flow

#### `for` — iterator loop

```ans
for (let element in formula) {
    mass += element.atomic_mass * formula[element];
}
```

#### `if` / `elif` / `else`

```ans
if (mass > 18.0) {
    print "Heavy.";
}
elif (mass == 18.0) {
    print "Exactly 18.";
}
else {
    print "Light.";
}
```

All branch bodies are braced blocks — there is no dangling-else ambiguity.

#### `print`

```ans
print "The yield is positive.";
print molar_mass(water);
```

### Expressions

Operator precedence (lowest to highest):

| Level | Operators |
|---|---|
| Comparison | `==` `!=` `>=` `<=` `>` `<` |
| Additive | `+` `-` |
| Multiplicative | `*` `/` |
| Unary | `-` |
| Postfix | call `()`, index `[]`, member `.` |
| Primary | literals, identifiers, `(expr)` |

Binary `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` are left-associative. A single comparison is allowed per expression (no chaining).

Member access and indexing:

```ans
c.formula          // property access
formula[element]   // index access
molar_mass(water)  // function call
```

### Literals

| Kind | Examples |
|---|---|
| Number | `20`, `1.008`, `21.2`, `890.3`, `6.02e23` |
| String | `"Water"`, `"Carbon dioxide"` |
| Character | `'H'`, `'\n'` |
| Formula | `H`, `O2`, `H2O`, `CH4`, `CO2` |
| Quantity | `5.0 mol`, `890.3 kJ/mol`, `18.0 g/mol` |
| List | `[H, O, C]`, `[1, "two", 3.45]` |

---

## Lexical Structure

ANS uses six token categories produced by a maximal-munch (longest-match) scanner followed by a reserved-word filter.

### Identifiers

```
[a-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*
```

User-defined names always start with a lowercase letter or `_`. Any token starting with an uppercase letter is classified as a **formula literal**, not an identifier — this is how `water` and `H2O` are kept visually and grammatically separate without extra keyword rules.

### Formula Literals

```
([A-Z][a-z]?[0-9]*)+
```

Examples: `H`, `O`, `Na`, `H2O`, `CH4`, `CO2`, `NaCl`. The lexer produces a single `FORMULA` token for a whole molecular formula; no lookahead or statefulness is required.

### Unit Literals

Compound units containing `/` are scanned as a single token before the `/` operator is considered:

```
kg/mol | g/mol | kJ/mol
```

Single-word units (`mol`, `g`, `kg`, `kJ`) are emitted as identifiers by the scanner and promoted to `<unit>` role by the parser only when they immediately follow a number literal.

### Keywords

**Hard reserved words** (may never be used as identifiers):

```
let  function  return  for  in  if  elif  else  print
```

**Contextual keywords** (valid identifiers in all other positions; promoted by the parser based on grammar context):

| Position | Words |
|---|---|
| Declaration head | `element` `compound` `reaction` |
| Declaration field names | `atomic_mass` `valence` `symbol` `formula` `name` `reactants` `products` `check` `energy` |
| Reaction field values | `balanced` `exothermic` `endothermic` |
| Parameter type annotations | `element` `compound` `reaction` |

### Operators

```
==  !=  <=  >=  +=  -=  *=  /=  =  +  -  *  /  <  >
```

### Separators

```
{  }  (  )  [  ]  ,  ;  .
```

### Comments

Line comments only, discarded before parsing:

```
// This is a comment
```

## Grammar (EBNF Summary)

```ebnf
<program>             → { <top_level_statement> } EOF

<top_level_statement> → <element_declaration> ";"
                      | <compound_declaration> ";"
                      | <reaction_declaration> ";"
                      | <function_declaration> ";"
                      | <variable_declaration> ";"
                      | <print_statement> ";"
                      | <expression_statement> ";"
                      | <if_statement>
                      | <for_statement>

<element_declaration> → "element" <formula_literal> "{" <element_field_list> "}"
<element_field>       → "atomic_mass" "=" <number_literal>
                      | "valence"     "=" <number_literal>
                      | "symbol"      "=" <string_literal>

<compound_declaration>→ "compound" <identifier> "{" <compound_field_list> "}"
<compound_field>      → "formula" "=" <formula_literal>
                      | "name"    "=" <string_literal>

<reaction_declaration>→ "reaction" <identifier> "{" <reaction_field_list> "}"
<reaction_field>      → "reactants" "=" <reaction_expression>
                      | "products"  "=" <reaction_expression>
                      | "check"     "=" "balanced"
                      | "energy"    "=" ( "exothermic" | "endothermic" ) <quantity_literal>

<reaction_expression> → <reaction_term> { "+" <reaction_term> }
<reaction_term>       → <species_ref> | <number_literal> "*" <species_ref>
<species_ref>         → <formula_literal> | <identifier>

<function_declaration>→ "function" <identifier> "(" [ <parameter_list> ] ")" <block>
<parameter>           → [ <type_name> ] <identifier>
<type_name>           → "element" | "compound" | "reaction"

<for_statement>       → "for" "(" "let" <identifier> "in" <expression> ")" <block>
<if_statement>        → "if" "(" <expression> ")" <block>
                        { "elif" "(" <expression> ")" <block> }
                        [ "else" <block> ]

<expression>          → <comparison_expression>
<comparison_expression> → <additive_expression>
                          [ ( "==" | "!=" | ">=" | "<=" | ">" | "<" ) <additive_expression> ]
<additive_expression> → <multiplicative_expression> { ( "+" | "-" ) <multiplicative_expression> }
<multiplicative_expression> → <unary_expression> { ( "*" | "/" ) <unary_expression> }
<unary_expression>    → [ "-" ] <postfix_expression>
<postfix_expression>  → <primary_expression> { "." <identifier> | "[" <expression> "]" | "(" [ <argument_list> ] ")" }
<primary_expression>  → <number_or_quantity_literal> | <string_literal> | <char_literal>
                      | <formula_literal> | <list_literal> | <identifier>
                      | "(" <expression> ")"

<number_or_quantity_literal> → <number_literal> [ <unit> ]
<unit>                → UNIT_LITERAL | "mol" | "g" | "kg" | "kJ"
<list_literal>        → "[" [ <argument_list> ] "]"
```

The full EBNF is in `D1/4.3/EBNF/ANS_complete_EBNF.ebnf`.

---

## Names, Scoping, and Lifetime

**Case sensitivity.** ANS is fully case-sensitive. Tokens starting with uppercase are always formula literals; lowercase-starting tokens are identifiers. There is no ambiguity.

**Static (lexical) scoping.** Every name resolves to the nearest enclosing declaration in the source text, outward to the top-level program scope. This is required for compile-time formula validation and balance checking — the compiler must resolve names from source text alone without simulating execution.

**Compile-time vs. run-time bindings:**

| Binding | When |
|---|---|
| Operator symbol → semantics | Language-design time |
| Lexeme → token category | Compile time (lex) |
| Identifier → declaration | Compile time (static scope walk) |
| Variable → inferred type | Compile time |
| Parameter → declared type | Compile time |
| Formula validity | Compile time |
| `check = balanced` | Compile time |
| Parameter → argument value | Run time (call) |
| Local variable → storage cell | Run time (block entry) |
| Loop variable → current element | Run time (each iteration) |

**Storage lifetimes:**

| Entity | Lifetime |
|---|---|
| `element`, `compound`, `reaction` declarations | Static — allocated once, live for the whole program |
| Top-level `let` variables | Static |
| Function parameters | Stack-dynamic — allocated per call, supports recursion |
| Local `let` inside a function/block | Stack-dynamic — freed on block exit |
| `for` loop variable | Stack-dynamic — one allocation for the loop, rebound each iteration |
| List/compound/reaction values | Implicit heap-dynamic (runtime-managed, no explicit `new`/`delete`) |

ANS has **no explicit-heap-dynamic storage**, no pointers, and no aliasing, eliminating use-after-free and dangling-pointer errors by design.

---

## Implementation

The current implementation is a hand-written C11 front end (lexer + parser + AST) in `D2/`.

### Components

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `src/lexer.c` | Maximal-munch scanner: whitespace/comment skipping, formula/unit/keyword scanning |
| `src/parser.c` | Recursive-descent parser — one function per EBNF rule |
| `src/ast.c` | AST node constructors and tree pretty-printer |
| `src/error.c` | `<file>:<line>:<col>: error:` formatting |
| `src/main.c` | CLI entry point: reads file, runs lexer + parser, optionally dumps AST |

### Parser strategy

The parser is a single-token lookahead recursive-descent parser matching the EBNF grammar exactly. Panic-mode error recovery skips to the next `;`, `}`, or EOF on any syntax error, allowing multiple errors to be reported per run.

**Contextual keyword disambiguation** happens entirely in the parser: `element`, `compound`, and `reaction` are contextual, resolved as declaration keywords vs. type annotations based on grammar position. The lexer emits plain `IDENT` for all three.

**Formula vs. identifier disambiguation** is done in the lexer by case: uppercase-leading → `FORMULA`, lowercase/`_`-leading → `IDENT`.

**Unit disambiguation**: compound units (`g/mol`, `kg/mol`, `kJ/mol`) are probed before consuming `/`, so they are emitted as `UNIT_LIT` without lexer statefulness. Single-word units (`mol`, `g`, `kg`, `kJ`) are always `IDENT`; the parser recognises them as `<unit>` only when they follow a number.
